narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year grades, which placed you in the second decile of your class. This was substantially weaker than the average student who was accepted (around the sixth decile). That low ranking strongly pushed the model toward predicting you would fail the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor. At 3.20 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this small difference actually worked mildly in your favor, nudging the prediction slightly toward passing.

The third most influential piece of information was your first-year grades, which also placed you in the second decile—far below the sixth-decile average of accepted applicants. This again pushed the prediction toward failure.

Taken together, your consistently lower class rankings in law school outweighed the small positive signal from your GPA and led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking key courses or seeking additional bar-preparation support before reapplying. Improving your class rank would have the biggest impact on future predictions. (248 words)
